extracted.intended_audience: students, lawmakers, and readers interested in constitutional design and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_short: design of elections and federal judiciary
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and practical criteria for configuring an elective executive and a national judiciary—covering dangers of electing a powerful executive, electoral-mode design (special electors, sealed simultaneous votes, House choice among top three), effects of re-election, administrative turnover, and the need, structure, and independence of federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of elective system increase with executive prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: “The dangers of the system of election applied to the head of the executive government of a great people ... may be more or less formidable in proportion to the place which the executive power occupies, and to the importance it possesses in the State.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that an elective office offers a lure to private ambition; the greater the privileges of the executive, the greater the temptation, and thus the greater the danger (example: Polish revolutions). Implication: if an executive is to be elective, its prerogatives should be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of an elective executive depends on people and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: “Before we can discuss the absolute advantages of the elective system we must make preliminary inquiries as to whether the geographical position, the laws, the habits, the manners, and the opinions of the people amongst whom it is to be introduced will admit of the establishment of a weak and dependent executive government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must assess physical, legal, social, and cultural conditions before adopting an elective executive; what works in America (vast territory, no hostile neighbors, people used to freedom) may not work elsewhere. Republican hatred of tyranny can obscure recognition that limiting executive power may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: To render a formerly hereditary sovereign safely elective, circumscribe and diminish prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: “To reduce hereditary royalty to the condition of an elective authority, the only means that I am acquainted with are to circumscribe its sphere of action beforehand, gradually to diminish its prerogatives, and to accustom the people to live without its protection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If converting monarchy to elective rule, do so by progressively limiting powers and weaning populace from reliance on executive protection; abrupt transition to a powerful elective sovereign is deemed incompatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective system inherently introduces instability into policy
rubrics_metrics.description: “One of the principal vices of the elective system is that it always introduces a certain degree of instability into the internal and external policy of the State. But this disadvantage is less sensibly felt if the share of power vested in the elected magistrate is small.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the trade-off: frequent change in holders of executive office tends to change policy unless counterbalanced by other stable institutions (e.g., Rome’s hereditary Senate). Implication: concentrate directing authority elsewhere (assemblies, senate) to preserve fixed principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections create temporary suspension of government action (national crisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The wheels of government cease to act, as it were, at the approach of an election ... At the approach of an election the head of the executive government is wholly occupied by the coming struggle; his future plans are doubtful; he can undertake nothing new...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must recognize the election period as a national crisis whose danger scales with internal and external threats. Translator’s notes caution that in extreme cases (e.g., Buchanan–Lincoln interregnum) paralysis during transition can be catastrophic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility of the executive increases intrigue and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “Intrigue and corruption are the natural defects of elective government; but when the head of the State can be re-elected these evils rise to a great height ... the State itself, with all its immense influence, is busied in the work of corruption and cabal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that allowing re-election leads incumbents to use government instruments for personal electoral advantage, turning public offices and actions into electioneering tools. Suggests ineligibility (or limits) would help maintain executive independence and reduce corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnover of removable public officers at each election produces administrative revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: “The consequence of this arrangement is, that at every new election the fate of all the Federal public officers is in suspense ... to substitute one system for another, as is done in America every four years, by law, is to cause a sort of revolution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that presidential power to appoint and remove agents creates broad personnel churn on regime change; while less harmful in the US because independent livelihood is easy, high turnover is nevertheless disruptive and resembles systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate election to a special electoral body to reduce excitement and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “Their object was to find the mode of election which would best express the choice of the people with the least possible excitement and suspense... to delegate the electoral powers of the nation to a body of representatives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale for the electoral college: fewer electors make majority outcomes more probable; special electors are less exposed to pre-election corruption than legislators; electors vote separately and on the same day to minimize cabal and delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards for the electoral college and contingency rules
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was determined that the electors should all vote upon the same day, without being convoked to the same place... the votes should be transmitted sealed to the President of the Senate, and that they should be opened and counted in the presence of the Senate and the House of Representatives. If none of the candidates has a majority, the House of Representatives then proceeds immediately to elect a President ... it must fix upon one of the three candidates who have the highest numbers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies concrete procedural measures: simultaneous voting, sealed transmission, congressional counting, and House selection among the top three as contingency to avoid prolonged uncertainty (illustrated by Jefferson’s 36 ballots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature should not elect the chief magistrate because of exposure to manoeuvres
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was thought that if the legislature was empowered to elect the head of the executive power, its members would, for some time before the election, be exposed to the manoeuvres of corruption and the tricks of intrigue; whereas the special electors would, like a jury, remain mixed up with the crowd till the day of action...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains preference for a distinct electoral assembly rather than letting the lawmaking body elect the executive; the latter would invite sustained manipulation of legislators prior to an election.

rubrics_metrics.name: A federal government requires a national judiciary to enforce its laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “A federal government stands in greater need of the support of judicial institutions than any other, because it is naturally weak and exposed to formidable opposition... The Union, therefore, required a national judiciary to enforce the obedience of the citizens to the laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the moral force of courts is essential to substitute law for violence and to make enforcement practicable for a weak federal authority; without federal courts the Union could not apply its laws uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts are unsuitable to enforce federal law due to partiality and multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: “To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals instituted by these political bodies would be to allow foreign judges to preside over the nation... the number, still more than the mere character, of the tribunals of the States rendered them unfit for the service of the nation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out two defects in using state courts: judges would be 'foreign' and partial to their state interests, and numerous differing tribunals would create conflicting interpretations that undermine national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and independence of the federal judiciary (Supreme Court and inferior courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The entire judicial power of the Union was centred in one tribunal, which was denominated the Supreme Court of the United States. ... inferior courts were appended to it... The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. In order to render them independent of the other authorities, their office was made inalienable; and it was determined that their salary, when once fixed, should not be altered by the legislature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies appointment method, life tenure (inalienable office), and protection of salary to secure judicial independence; describes district and circuit courts for expedition of business and Supreme Court’s role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court should decide both fact and law (broader remit than some continental courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: “It will be observed that no analogy exists between the Supreme Court of the United States and the French Cour de Cassation, since the latter only hears appeals on questions of law. The Supreme Court decides upon the evidence of the fact as well as upon the law of the case ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that the US Supreme Court exercises a combined fact-and-law adjudicatory function (not merely cassation), affecting how appeals and final national interpretations are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial moral authority is a necessary alternative to physical coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great end of justice is to substitute the notion of right for that of violence, and to place a legal barrier between the power of the government and the use of physical force... The moral force which courts of justice possess renders the introduction of physical force exceedingly rare...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the normative role of courts: legitimacy and compliance derive from perceived legal right and judicial decisions, reducing reliance on force; this underpins why a national judiciary is central to stable federal governance.
